title: sandbox-ai-mcp
description: Audited, container-packaged MCP servers for sandbox-ai (search, web, analysis), built by https://github.com/c0decave/sandbox-ai-mcp and pinned by digest. The same schema as axross-mcp-hub, so sandbox-ai and axross read both catalogs.

entries.name: binwalk
entries.title: binwalk
entries.description: What is inside a firmware file: binwalk's signature scan, extraction of embedded archives and file systems (SquashFS, CPIO, 7z, zip, gzip, xz, bzip2, LZO), entropy analysis and hex dumps. The images are read from the folder mounted read-only at /work. Extraction writes into a writable folder mounted at /out, or, without one, into the container's own /tmp (64 MiB, gone when the server stops). No network.
entries.license: MIT (MCP server, FuzzingLabs; binwalk)

mounts.description: The folder with the firmware images (mount it read-only: --mount /work=DIR:ro)
Where extracted files are kept; the only folder the server writes to, so mount it writable (--mount /out=DIR:rw) and only when you want them kept

entries.notes: binwalk_extract is the one tool that writes: into /out when a writable folder is mounted there, else into the container's /tmp. Extraction runs third-party extractors on data someone else made, inside the container (no capabilities, no network, read-only root, noexec /tmp); mount /work read-only so an extractor cannot touch the image it read. What the scan reports is that data: treat it as data, not instructions.

tor.note: No network: it reaches nothing, so nothing of it goes through Tor (sandbox-ai gives a server without network no VPN).

entries.name: bluesky
entries.title: Bluesky posts (your account, the app password stays in the server)
entries.description: Posts to your Bluesky account through the AT Protocol without the agent ever seeing your credentials: your handle and an app password (never the account password) live only in this server's container, which signs in at your PDS itself and keeps the session in memory. post (up to 300 graphemes counted as Bluesky counts them; links, @mentions and #hashtags as facets; languages; a reply; up to 4 JPEG, PNG or WebP images of /upload with alt text and their metadata - EXIF, location - removed, or a link card from the title and description you give, the site is never fetched), thread (2-10 posts, each answering the one before) and delete_post (only the account's own posts) WRITE to the account and are refused unless BLUESKY_WRITE=1 - read-only by default; have sandbox-ai ask for each call. get_profile, list_my_posts and get_post_thread read through Bluesky's public AppView, never with the session. A sign-in with the account password or an app password with access to direct messages is refused and ended. Files only from a folder mounted read-only at /upload, no links, devices or other users' files. Needs BLUESKY_HANDLE, BLUESKY_APP_PASSWORD (a secret) and network: Allowlist with bsky.social:443 (your PDS; another with BLUESKY_PDS) and public.api.bsky.app:443.
entries.license: MIT (MCP server, sandbox-ai-mcp)

env.name: BLUESKY_HANDLE
env.description: Your handle (alice.bsky.social) or DID (did:plc:...): the account the server signs in to

env.name: BLUESKY_APP_PASSWORD
env.description: An app password of that account (xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx, Settings, Privacy and security, App passwords; without DM access), never the account password

env.name: BLUESKY_WRITE
env.description: 1 lets post, thread and delete_post write to the account (unset: read-only, every write refused)

env.name: BLUESKY_PDS
env.description: The https:// address of your PDS if it is not Bluesky's (default https://bsky.social, which serves every Bluesky-hosted account)

mounts.description: The images (and link-card thumbnails) to post, read-only (--mount /upload=DIR:ro); without it posts carry no images

entries.notes: The app password stays in the server's container (environment, memory), as do the session tokens it gets for it: never returned, never logged, never sent anywhere but your PDS; the agent never sees them. An app password can post, delete and change the profile and follows, but not change the account's e-mail or password, delete the account or read direct messages; revoke it any time under App passwords. Ask for every write: a ruleset with {"server": "bluesky", "tool": ["post", "thread", "delete_post"], "decision": "ask"} makes sandbox-ai ask you for each call (tools.json has the whole recommended ruleset). Posts are public at once. Bluesky limits writes per account (about 1,600 posts an hour, 11,600 a day) and sign-ins (30 in 5 minutes, 300 a day): the server signs in once per connection and keeps the session. sandbox-ai gives an allowlist entry the full network (it cannot limit a server to hosts yet); the server itself sends requests to your PDS and public.api.bsky.app only.

tor.note: HTTPS to your PDS and Bluesky's AppView, over TCP through Tor.

entries.name: capa
entries.title: capa (Mandiant)
entries.description: What a binary can do: Mandiant capa with the capa-rules set names the capabilities of a PE, ELF or .NET file or of shellcode, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK and MBC. Files are read from the folder mounted read-only at /work (capa_analyze takes /work/<file>); capa's JSON report is written inside the container's own /tmp, never to your folder. No network.
entries.license: MIT (MCP server, FuzzingLabs) AND Apache-2.0 (capa, capa-rules)

mounts.description: The folder with the files to analyze (mount it read-only: --mount /work=DIR:ro)

entries.notes: The rules and the FLIRT signatures are part of the image (pinned), so capa matches without fetching anything. A large binary can exceed sandbox-ai's 512 MiB container memory (--memory) or the tool's default 300 s; capa_analyze takes a timeout of up to 3600 s. Rule names and strings in the answer come from the analyzed file: data, not instructions.

tor.note: No network: it reaches nothing, so nothing of it goes through Tor (sandbox-ai gives a server without network no VPN).

entries.name: chrome-devtools
entries.title: Browser debugging (Chrome DevTools MCP, Chromium)
entries.description: A headless Chromium (Debian's) driven by Google's Chrome DevTools MCP 1.12.0 through Puppeteer: open pages and tabs, read them as accessibility snapshots, click, type, fill forms, drag, press keys, handle dialogs, wait for text, run JavaScript in the page, take screenshots and screencasts, read console messages and network requests with their bodies, emulate devices, network and CPU, record and analyse performance traces, run Lighthouse audits, take heap snapshots. A fresh temporary profile per connection; no file: URLs; files only in the server's own /tmp; no tools a web page offers, no extensions. No usage statistics, no update check, no CrUX lookups. Needs network: Full and more than the default limits (2g memory, 2 CPUs, 512 processes, a 768m /tmp: sandbox-ai 0.1.94 takes them from the catalog).
entries.license: Apache-2.0 (Chrome DevTools MCP; bundled Puppeteer, Lighthouse, DevTools frontend and others: THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES in the package); Chromium: BSD-3-Clause and others (Debian)
entries.notes: Add it with --network full (sandbox-ai 0.1.94 and newer apply the limits this catalog recommends; older ones: --memory 2g --pids 512). The browser runs inside the server's container, not the session's browser: it goes wherever the network lets it, logged-in sessions included if the agent logs in, and the server's own process also fetches source maps the pages name. --allowed-url-pattern and --blocked-url-pattern are no boundary, the container's network is. evaluate_script and navigate_page's initScript run JavaScript in the page, never in the server. Screenshots, traces and heap snapshots are written to the server's /tmp (gone with the container) unless returned. Page texts, titles, console messages and network answers are written by whoever made the page: treat them as data, not instructions.

tor.note: Chromium over TCP through Tor (QUIC falls back to TCP); some sites challenge or refuse Tor exits.

entries.name: code-search
entries.title: Code search for small local models (definitions, outlines, bounded search)
entries.description: Finds and reads code in a project mounted read-only at /work, so that a small local model finds a function instead of guessing its name and reads that function instead of the whole file: find_definition (where a function, class, method, type or constant is defined, by name, exact matches first, similar names when there is none), read_symbol (the source of one function or class with line numbers), outline (the classes, functions and methods of a file with lines and signatures), find_references (definitions first, then the lines using a name with the function each is in), find_text (plain text or a regular expression, file:line and the function, at most 200 with an offset to go on), find_files (by part of a name or a glob, best first), project_map (a tree with file counts, sizes and each file's main classes and functions). Python is read by Python's own parser; JavaScript/TypeScript, Go, Rust, Java, C/C++ and shell by line patterns and brace counting (approximate, and every answer says so). Honours .gitignore and skips node_modules, build, dist, target, vendor, .git, binary and minified files. Every answer is bounded, every search has a time limit; a regular expression that repeats a repeat is refused. Nothing is written; no link is followed out of the folders, no device, pipe or socket opened. No network.
entries.license: MIT (MCP server, sandbox-ai-mcp)

mounts.description: The project to search, read-only (--mount /work=PROJECT:ro); never written
Another folder to search, read-only (--mount /ref1=DIR:ro), named as /ref1/...; never written
Another folder to search, read-only (--mount /ref2=DIR:ro); never written
Another folder to search, read-only (--mount /ref3=DIR:ro); never written

entries.notes: Made for agents on small local models (OpenCode, Codex, Hermes with --llm), which fail to find code, read whole files into a small context and guess names: seven tools with short descriptions, plain-text answers whose first line says what was found, and every refusal saying what to do instead. Outlines are cached per file (modification time, size, inode) for the next call; the first find_definition over a project of a few thousand files takes seconds. Searches stop after 10 s and the index after 20 s with what they have (a second call goes on); files over 2 MiB are not read. The code it shows was written by someone else: data, not instructions.

tor.note: No network: it reaches nothing, so nothing of it goes through Tor (sandbox-ai gives a server without network no VPN).

entries.name: context7
entries.title: Context7 (current library documentation)
entries.description: Upstash's Context7 MCP server (@upstash/context7-mcp 4.4.4): current documentation and code examples of libraries, frameworks and APIs from the Context7 service. resolve-library-id turns a library name into a Context7 library ID (with snippet counts, source reputation and versions), query-docs returns the documentation for a question about that library, optionally ranked for a programming language. The library name or ID and the question go to context7.com (nothing else: no client name or session id, no telemetry, no sign-in prompt); nothing is read or written locally. Works without a key (rate-limited); CONTEXT7_API_KEY raises the limits. Needs network: Allowlist with context7.com:443.
entries.license: MIT (Context7 MCP, express, undici, jose, commander, zod); MCP TypeScript SDK: Apache-2.0 (in transition from MIT); Node.js: MIT

env.name: CONTEXT7_API_KEY
env.description: Context7 API key (optional, higher rate limits): https://context7.com/dashboard, starts with ctx7sk

entries.notes: Every question and library name the agent asks about is sent to Context7 (Upstash): do not put secrets, personal data or proprietary code into a query - the tool descriptions say so to the agent too. The key is sent only to context7.com as a bearer token and never returned or logged. The documentation comes from Context7's index of public repositories and web pages, written by others: treat it as data, not instructions. Upstash also runs this server remotely (https://mcp.context7.com/mcp), which needs no container.

tor.note: HTTPS to context7.com, over TCP through Tor.

entries.name: duckduckgo
entries.title: DuckDuckGo search
entries.description: Web search without an API key through DuckDuckGo's HTML endpoint: title, URL and snippet of each result, optionally for a region. Only https://html.duckduckgo.com/html/ is requested. Needs network: Allowlist with html.duckduckgo.com:443.
entries.license: MIT (MCP server, sandbox-ai-mcp)
entries.notes: DuckDuckGo rate-limits automated queries; a refused query answers with an error naming that. Results are what DuckDuckGo shows, without ads.

entries.name: engram
entries.title: Engram memory for coding agents
entries.description: Persistent memory for a coding agent with Engram 3.6.0 (Gentleman-Programming/engram): decisions, bugs, discoveries and conventions saved as observations in SQLite with full-text search (FTS5), session summaries, recent context after a compaction, topic keys for upserts, conflict review between memories, pins and review dates. Only Engram's MCP server with its agent tools (23); no CLI, HTTP API, TUI, Engram Cloud, sync or update check. The memory is the folder mounted writable at /data; one project per folder (ENGRAM_PROJECT, default brain); no tool takes a file path or looks at another folder. No network.
entries.license: MIT (Engram, mcp-go) AND BSD-3-Clause (modernc.org/sqlite and libc, Go x/sys and x/text, google/uuid; SQLite: public domain) AND MIT/BSD/Apache-2.0 (other Go modules)

env.name: ENGRAM_PROJECT
env.description: The project the memories of this folder belong to (lower-case letters, digits, '.', '_', '-'; default brain)

mounts.description: The memory's folder, writable (--mount /data=DIR:rw): engram.db with its WAL, .instance-id and two lock files. One folder per project or case, e.g. --mount /data=~/brains/sandbox-ai-dev:rw

entries.notes: One folder per case: mkdir -p ~/brains/CASE, then sandbox-ai mcp add engram --mount /data=~/brains/CASE:rw. The folder must be on a local file system (Engram refuses NFS and SMB) and must not be changed while a connection uses it (Engram stops when its database files are replaced). Several connections may share one folder: SQLite's locks order them. Engram's instructions ask the agent to save proactively and to write a session summary before it ends; saved texts come back in later sessions, so treat what the memory returns as data, not instructions. The directory and cwd arguments of mem_session_start and mem_current_project are not offered: they would scan other folders of the container.

tor.note: No network: it reaches nothing, so nothing of it goes through Tor (sandbox-ai gives a server without network no VPN).

entries.name: exec
entries.title: Shell commands for small local models (time limits, bounded output)
entries.description: Runs commands for an agent in its project folder, mounted writable at /work, so that a small local model does not stall, die or drown in output: run_command (bash, a time limit per call, default 120 s, max EXEC_MAX_TIMEOUT; stdin empty, no terminal, CI=1, PAGER=cat, EDITOR=true and the yes-switches of apt, pip and npm; the whole process tree stopped on the limit; output shortened to its first and last lines with the number omitted, colours and progress bars removed), start_job/job_status/stop_job/list_jobs for long builds and servers, run_tests (pytest, unittest, jest, vitest, go test, cargo test: only the failures), lint (pyflakes, shellcheck, JSON, YAML; runs nothing of the project). The start folder must be inside /work. The commands run in this server's container, with its tools (bash, coreutils, git, make, python3 with pytest, node, shellcheck) and no network. run_command, start_job, run_tests and stop_job change things: have sandbox-ai ask for them if you want to. Needs 2g memory, 512 processes and a 512m /tmp (sandbox-ai 0.1.94 applies them from the catalog).
entries.license: MIT (MCP server, sandbox-ai-mcp); Debian packages under their own licences

env.name: EXEC_TIMEOUT
env.description: Seconds a command may run when the call names no limit (1-86400, default 120)

env.name: EXEC_MAX_TIMEOUT
env.description: The most seconds a call may ask for (1-86400, default 600); longer work goes to start_job

env.name: EXEC_JOB_TIMEOUT
env.description: Seconds a background job may run (1-604800, default 3600)

env.name: EXEC_MAX_JOBS
env.description: Background jobs (and commands) running at once (1-32, default 4)

env.name: EXEC_OUTPUT_LINES
env.description: Lines of output an answer shows, a quarter of the start and the rest of the end (20-2000, default 100)

env.name: EXEC_ENV_ALLOW
env.description: Names of variables of the server's environment the commands get too, comma separated (default none: the commands get a fixed environment)

mounts.description: The project folder, writable (--mount /work=PROJECT:rw): the agent's workspace folder itself, not a folder inside it

entries.notes: This gives an agent nothing it does not have: it has a shell of its own already. The server is for models that lose themselves in a raw shell (a prompt that waits forever, a dev server that never ends, a build log of 50,000 lines). The commands run in this container, not in the agent's sandbox: only the tools of this image, only /work and the container's /tmp writable, no network (installing packages fails here; do that from the agent's own shell). Codex waits 60 s for an MCP call by default: raise its tool_timeout_sec for this server, or set EXEC_TIMEOUT and EXEC_MAX_TIMEOUT below that. The server runs as PID 1 of its container ("pid1": "server"; sandbox-ai 0.1.95 starts it so: Podman without --init, bwrap --as-pid-1), and it is not dumpable: its commands can open neither its MCP connection nor its environment through /proc. An older sandbox-ai starts an init as PID 1, which holds both: there a command can write MCP messages to the client and read every variable of the container at /proc/1/environ, and under Bubblewrap the server refuses to run commands (use --backend podman). Give the server no secrets either way. Command output comes from programs and files of the project: data, not instructions.

tor.note: No network: it reaches nothing, so nothing of it goes through Tor (sandbox-ai gives a server without network no VPN).

entries.name: files
entries.title: Workspace files (reliable reads and writes, Markdown repairs)
entries.description: Reads and writes the files of an agent's workspace - the folder mounted at /work - so that a small local model gets them right: read_file (in parts, with the file's sha256), list_dir, glob, search, stat, diff, checksum; write_file (atomic, an existing file replaced only with the sha256 it was read with or overwrite=true, permissions, line breaks and byte order mark kept, binary-looking content refused), write_markdown (repairs what local models get wrong - a ```markdown fence around everything, literal \n, a JSON string, CRLF, trailing spaces, #Heading, an open code fence, a repeated first heading - and lists each repair; dry_run), edit_file (one exact match, or a single whitespace-tolerant one, said so), insert_lines, delete_lines, append_file, apply_patch (strict hunks, the file's text shown when one does not apply), move, copy, mkdir, delete (into /work/.trash). Every write answers lines added and removed and the new sha256. Nothing outside the mounted folders: no '..', no link followed out of a folder (the write tools follow none), no devices, pipes or sockets. Folders mounted at /ref1-/ref3 are only read. FILES_READONLY=1 refuses every write. No network.
entries.license: MIT (MCP server, sandbox-ai-mcp)

env.name: FILES_READONLY
env.description: 1: every write tool refuses (the server only reads)

env.name: FILES_MAX_BYTES
env.description: Bytes one call reads or writes, 1K to 256M (like 8M; default 8M)

env.name: FILES_TRASH
env.description: 0: delete removes for good instead of moving into /work/.trash (default 1)

mounts.description: The workspace, writable (--mount /work=PROJECT:rw; :ro makes it read-only): the only folder written
Another folder to read from, read-only (--mount /ref1=DIR:ro); never written
Another folder to read from, read-only (--mount /ref2=DIR:ro); never written
Another folder to read from, read-only (--mount /ref3=DIR:ro); never written

entries.notes: Made for agents on small local models (OpenCode, Codex, Hermes with --llm) that get file writes wrong: whole-file writes need the sha256 read_file gave (no blind clobbering), edits need one exact match, and write_markdown repairs and reports. The workspace may be the very project folder the agent works in (sandbox-ai refuses a folder inside a tree a sandbox can write, not that folder itself); one entry per project (sandbox-ai mcp add files --as files-NAME). Writes are atomic (temporary file, fsync, rename) and never through a link; .git and .trash are not written. Recommended: allow the read tools, ask for delete and move, or give FILES_READONLY=1 where the agent should only read.

tor.note: No network: it reaches nothing, so nothing of it goes through Tor (sandbox-ai gives a server without network no VPN).

entries.name: filesystem
entries.title: Filesystem (official MCP server)
entries.description: The official MCP filesystem server (@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem 2.1.0) on the folders you mount, nothing else: read_text_file (whole, head or tail), read_media_file (base64 image, audio or blob), read_multiple_files, write_file, edit_file (exact or whitespace-tolerant replacements, answered with a git-style diff; dryRun), create_directory, list_directory, list_directory_with_sizes, directory_tree (JSON), move_file, search_files (glob on names), get_file_info (size, times, permissions, hard links), list_allowed_directories. The allowed directories are exactly the folders mounted at /work and /ref1-/ref3 (an empty mount point is not allowed); MCP Roots are never used, so a client cannot widen them. Symbolic links out of them are refused, writes go through the checked directory and never through a link. No network.

mounts.description: The folder the server works on (--mount /work=FOLDER:rw to write, :ro to only read)
Another folder, best read-only (--mount /ref1=DIR:ro); a writable one is written too
Another folder, best read-only (--mount /ref2=DIR:ro); a writable one is written too

entries.notes: For agents on capable models that work with the reference tool set (Claude Desktop-style clients, agents written against it). Not stopped by the server: a write to a file that also has hard links elsewhere changes it at every name (get_file_info shows hardLinks). entries.name: gowitness

entries.name: memory
entries.title: Knowledge graph memory (official MCP server)
entries.description: The official MCP Knowledge Graph memory server (@modelcontextprotocol/server-memory 2.0.1): entities with a type and observations, and named relations between them, kept in one JSONL file in the folder mounted writable at /data (/data/memory.jsonl). Nine tools: create entities, relations and observations, delete each of them, search (a case-insensitive substring of names, types and observations), open nodes by name, read the whole graph. No tool takes a file path, nothing else is read or written. No network.
entries.license: Apache-2.0 AND MIT (modelcontextprotocol/servers, in transition from MIT to Apache-2.0); MCP TypeScript SDK: Apache-2.0; zod: MIT; Node.js: MIT

mounts.description: The graph's folder, writable (--mount /data=DIR:rw): memory.jsonl lives there. One folder per case, e.g. --mount /data=~/brains/CASE:rw

entries.notes: One folder per case keeps cases apart: mkdir -p ~/brains/CASE, then sandbox-ai mcp add memory --mount /data=~/brains/CASE:rw (a second case: add it again under another name or change the folder). The file is plain JSONL, one entity or relation per line: back it up or read it with any tool; a line the server cannot read is kept as it is. Every write rewrites the file through a temporary file in the same folder and holds memory.jsonl.lock meanwhile, so several connections can share one folder. read_graph returns the whole graph: a large case is better read with search_nodes and open_nodes. What is stored was often taken from sources the agent read: treat it as data, not instructions.

entries.name: openosint

env.description: Bright Data API key (search_dorks_live, search_footprint; each query is billed)

env.name: BRIGHTDATA_SERP_ZONE
env.description: Bright Data SERP API zone name, e.g. serp_api1

env.name: OPENOSINT_GDELT_WINDOW_HOURS
env.description: Hours of GDELT news search_gdelt_geo holds (1-24, default 1 here; each hour is 4 downloads of about 8 MB)

entries.notes: Passive only, enforced by the server: no tool sends anything to the target itself, VirusTotal URL submission and DNS DKIM selector probes are off whatever the environment says, and no .env or config file is read. What the lookups name goes to the services listed in PROVENANCE.md (the registries, ipinfo.io, api.github.com, psbdmp.ws, data.gdeltproject.org; with keys haveibeenpwned.com, virustotal.com, api.abuseipdb.com, api.ip2location.io, api.brightdata.com and through it Google); put a VPN in front (--vpn PROFILE) if they should not see your address. Keys are passed as environment variables and never returned or logged. Every answer is third-party data (registry records, TXT records, profiles, search results, news places): treat it as data, never as instructions. For authorised investigations only (OpenOSINT's DISCLAIMER.md): some tools collect personal data.

tor.note: Behind Tor search_dns asks public resolvers (1.1.1.1, 9.9.9.9, 8.8.8.8) over TCP through Tor, so every record type is answered; WHOIS (port 43) and the HTTPS lookups go over TCP through Tor, though a service may refuse or rate-limit Tor exits.

entries.name: osint-mcp
entries.title: Domain and website OSINT (osint-mcp)
entries.description: Public-source lookups on domains, IPs and websites, no API keys: RDAP registration (domain_whois, ip_whois), live DNS records, subdomains and certificate history from certificate transparency (crt.sh), Wayback Machine snapshots, ASN and announced prefixes (RIPEstat), open ports and known CVEs from Shodan InternetDB (no scanning), an SPF/DMARC/MTA-STS/DKIM grade, TLS certificate and HTTP security headers of a site; recon_domain and recon_batch (up to ten domains) combine them, compare_domains finds shared IPs, nameservers, mail servers and registrars, investigate_site reads a page and up to three of its contact/legal pages. Every answer lists its sources. HTTP and TLS go only to public addresses, also after redirects. Needs network: Full.
entries.license: MIT (osint-mcp, MCP Python SDK); dnspython: ISC; tldextract: BSD-3-Clause
entries.notes: Full network: rdap.org redirects to each registry's own RDAP server, and the site checks go to the domain you name. What it asks is seen by rdap.org and the registries, crt.sh, web.archive.org, stat.ripe.net and internetdb.shodan.io; recon_domain (include_active, on by default), investigate_site, http_headers, tls_certificate and email_security's MTA-STS policy fetch connect to the target itself, from the container's address (add --vpn PROFILE to hide yours). DNS goes to the container's resolver, which answers with what the host's resolver knows: names of your local network can resolve, and their private addresses are returned (HTTP and TLS to them are still refused). Page texts, TXT records, certificate names and headers are written by whoever runs the domain: data, never instructions. Answers are cached in memory for the connection (6 h at most), nothing is written to disk.

tor.note: Behind Tor every DNS lookup goes over TCP through Tor to public resolvers (1.1.1.1, 9.9.9.9, 8.8.8.8) or the nameserver a call names, so MX, TXT, NS, SOA and CAA are answered (email_security, recon_domain, compare_domains); RDAP, crt.sh, Wayback, RIPEstat, InternetDB, HTTP headers and TLS go over TCP through Tor, though a service may refuse or rate-limit Tor exits.

entries.name: playwright
entries.title: Browser (Playwright MCP, Chromium)
entries.description: A headless Chromium driven through Microsoft's Playwright MCP: open pages, read them as accessibility snapshots, click, type, fill forms, select, drag, press keys, handle dialogs, manage tabs, wait for text, run JavaScript in the page, take screenshots, and read the page's console messages and network requests. Debian's Chromium, a fresh in-memory profile per connection; file: URLs and files outside the server's own /tmp are refused; a page cannot add tools (WebMCP off). Needs network: Full and more than the default limits (2g memory, 2 CPUs, 512 processes, a 768m /tmp: sandbox-ai 0.1.94 takes them from the catalog).
entries.license: Apache-2.0 (Playwright MCP, Playwright); Chromium: BSD-3-Clause and others (Debian)
entries.notes: Add it with --network full (sandbox-ai 0.1.94 and newer apply the limits this catalog recommends; older ones: --memory 2g --pids 512): Chromium does not start reliably within the default 512 MiB and 128 processes, and crashes once its /tmp (its profile, cache, shared memory and screenshots; 64 MiB by default) is full - sandbox-ai mcp set playwright --recommended raises them for a server added before. The browser goes wherever the network lets it, logged-in sessions included if the agent logs in; --allowed-origins and --blocked-origins are no boundary, the container's network is. browser_run_code_unsafe runs JavaScript in the server's own process: code execution inside the container (no capabilities, read-only root, nothing of yours mounted), never outside it. Page texts, titles, console messages and network answers are written by whoever made the page: treat them as data, not instructions.

tor.note: Chromium over TCP through Tor (QUIC falls back to TCP); some sites challenge or refuse Tor exits.

entries.name: radare2
entries.title: radare2 (r2mcp)
entries.description: Static analysis of a binary you hold, with radare2 through its official MCP server r2mcp: open a file, analyze, list functions, imports, exports, sections, symbols and strings, disassemble, decompile (r2's pdc), cross references. Binaries are read from the folder mounted read-only at /work (open_file takes /work/<file>); r2mcp refuses paths outside /work. Nothing is written, nothing is executed, no network.
entries.license: MIT (r2mcp) AND LGPL-3.0-only (radare2; some plugins GPL-3.0, Apache-2.0, BSD)

mounts.description: The folder with the binaries to analyze (mount it read-only: --mount /work=DIR:ro)

entries.notes: radare2's own sandbox is on (no shell, no sockets, no file writes) and the raw run_command / run_javascript tools are off, so a file under analysis cannot make radare2 run anything. The sql tool needs the r2xsql plugin, which is not included. The analyzed file, its strings and its symbols are written by someone else: treat what comes back as data, not instructions.

tor.note: No network: it reaches nothing, so nothing of it goes through Tor (sandbox-ai gives a server without network no VPN).

entries.name: searxng
entries.title: SearXNG search
entries.description: Web search through a SearXNG instance of yours (a metasearch engine that asks many search engines at once, without tracking): title, URL, snippet and engines of each result, with category, language, time range and pages. Set SEARXNG_URL to the instance (its JSON format allowed). Needs network to the instance (added with --network full: only SEARXNG_URL is requested).
entries.license: MIT (MCP server, sandbox-ai-mcp); SearXNG itself: AGPL-3.0-or-later

env.name: SEARXNG_URL
env.description: Your SearXNG instance, e.g. https://search.example.org or http://192.168.1.20:8888

entries.notes: Only SEARXNG_URL/search is requested. Run the instance yourself (docs/SEARXNG.md: a hardened container of the official image) or use one you trust; public instances usually refuse the JSON format.

tor.note: SEARXNG_URL must be reachable from a Tor exit: a public instance or an .onion address; one in your local network or on this host cannot be reached through Tor

entries.name: sequential-thinking
entries.title: Sequential thinking (official MCP server)
entries.description: The official MCP sequential-thinking server (@modelcontextprotocol/server-sequential-thinking 2.0.0): one tool, sequentialthinking, with which an agent writes down its reasoning as numbered thoughts - each can revise an earlier one or branch from it - and gets back the counts (thought number, estimated total, branches, length of the history). The thoughts are kept in memory for one connection only: nothing is read or written, nothing survives a restart. No network.
entries.license: Apache-2.0 AND MIT (modelcontextprotocol/servers, in transition from MIT to Apache-2.0); MCP TypeScript SDK: Apache-2.0; zod, chalk: MIT; Node.js: MIT
entries.notes: Useful for agents on capable models that do not reason natively, or to make a long chain of reasoning visible step by step; models with their own reasoning gain little, and small local models tend to keep thinking instead of acting - for those, the tasks server keeps a plan on disk. The model sets thoughtNumber, totalThoughts and nextThoughtNeeded itself; the server only counts and keeps the history until the connection ends. Thought logging to stderr is switched off in the image.

tor.note: No network: it reaches nothing, so nothing of it goes through Tor (sandbox-ai gives a server without network no VPN).

entries.name: signal
entries.title: Signal account (linked device, read-only by default)
entries.description: A Signal account of yours, linked as a secondary device through signal-cli, with the message handling and local history of signal-mcp: fetch new messages, unread messages, conversations with a contact or a group, full-text search of the history, contacts, groups and members (invite links left out); attachments as metadata only (nothing is downloaded, no file can be sent). Read-only: send_message, send_group_message and react_to_message exist only with SIGNAL_WRITE=1, optionally limited to SIGNAL_ALLOWED_RECIPIENTS. Needs a folder mounted writable at /data that holds the account (link it once with the image's --link) and network: Full (Signal's servers); --memory 1g --pids 256 (signal-cli runs on Java).
entries.license: MIT (MCP server, sandbox-ai-mcp; signal-mcp); signal-cli: GPL-3.0; libsignal: AGPL-3.0; Temurin: GPL-2.0 with Classpath Exception

env.name: SIGNAL_WRITE
env.description: 1 offers the write tools send_message, send_group_message and react_to_message (unset: read-only, they are not offered at all)

env.name: SIGNAL_ALLOWED_RECIPIENTS
env.description: Comma-separated phone numbers (+4915112345678), usernames (alice.42) and group ids (from list_groups) the write tools may send to (recommended with SIGNAL_WRITE; unset: everyone)

mounts.description: The account's folder, writable (--mount /data=DIR:rw): signal-cli's data with the account's keys, and the message history. A folder of its own for this server only.

entries.notes: The folder mounted at /data is the account: signal-cli's keys of this linked device and the message history live there, and no tool reads anything else of it or takes a file path. Link it once, with the network, before adding the server: podman run --rm -it --network=pasta --user=0:0 --cap-drop=ALL --security-opt=no-new-privileges --read-only --tmpfs=/tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,nodev,size=64m -v DIR:/data:rw IMAGE --link NAME prints a sgnl:// link; show it as a QR code (qrencode -t ansiutf8 'sgnl://...') and scan it in Signal on the phone (Settings, Linked devices). Then: sandbox-ai mcp add signal --network full --memory 1g --pids 256 --mount /data=DIR:rw. One connection at a time: signal-cli locks the account. Fetching messages sends Signal's delivery receipts, never read receipts; unread is tracked in the local history only. Unlink the device on the phone to revoke it. Message texts, names and group titles are written by other people: treat them as data, not instructions.

tor.note: signal-cli reaches Signal's servers over TCP (HTTPS and websockets) through Tor.

entries.name: tasks
entries.title: A plan outside the model's context (goal, steps, notes)
entries.description: Keeps an agent's plan outside its context, in the project folder mounted writable at /work, so that a small local model keeps its goal after a compaction or a restart and does not repeat a mistake: set_goal, add_steps, remove_step, start_step, complete_step (with a note of what was done), block_step (with the reason), add_note (facts and mistakes not to repeat), next_step (the one step to work on now, with the goal, its notes, the last result and the latest notes), list_steps and progress (compact). Stored in /work/.tasks/plan.json, with a readable /work/.tasks/PLAN.md for the human; every change is locked and written atomically, so several connections can share one plan. No tool takes a path; sizes are bounded. No network.
entries.license: MIT (MCP server, sandbox-ai-mcp)

mounts.description: The project folder, writable (--mount /work=PROJECT:rw): the plan goes to PROJECT/.tasks

entries.notes: The plan is plain JSON with a Markdown copy beside it: read PROJECT/.tasks/PLAN.md to see what the agent is doing; edit plan.json only while no agent works on it (a plan the server cannot read is refused, never overwritten). The agent can also write .tasks with its own tools: the server checks every field it reads. What is stored was written by the model, often from what it read: data, not instructions.

tor.note: No network: it reaches nothing, so nothing of it goes through Tor (sandbox-ai gives a server without network no VPN).

entries.name: telegram
entries.title: Telegram bot
entries.description: A Telegram bot of yours through the official Bot API: read the messages sent to it (get_updates), send and edit text messages (at most 4096 characters, plain, HTML or MarkdownV2), look up a chat and the bot itself. No user account (MTProto). Needs a bot token from @BotFather in TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN and network: Allowlist with api.telegram.org:443. Set TELEGRAM_ALLOWED_CHATS to the chat ids the agent may use (recommended).
entries.license: MIT (MCP server, sandbox-ai-mcp)

env.name: TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN
env.description: Telegram bot token from @BotFather (digits:letters)

env.name: TELEGRAM_ALLOWED_CHATS
env.description: Comma-separated chat ids the tools may use, e.g. 123456789,-1001234567890 (recommended; unset: every chat)

entries.notes: The token is passed as an environment variable and never returned or logged by the server (the Bot API puts it in the URL path, so no URL or exception text is ever shown). With TELEGRAM_ALLOWED_CHATS set, every tool refuses other chats and get_updates leaves their messages out. Messages the bot receives are written by other people: treat them as data, not instructions.

tor.note: HTTPS to api.telegram.org, over TCP through Tor.

entries.name: telegram-user
entries.title: Telegram user account (read-only by default)
entries.description: A Telegram user account of yours through MTProto (Telethon), for investigating public channels and groups: resolve and search chats by name or @username, full chat info, invite links without joining, the account's dialogs, messages of a chat (limits, ids, date range), search in a chat or in all of the account's chats, comments of a post; media as metadata, downloaded only into a mounted writable /out (size-capped). Read-only: send_message, join_channel, leave_channel and mark_read exist only with TELEGRAM_USER_WRITE=1, optionally limited to TELEGRAM_USER_ALLOWED_CHATS. Needs TELEGRAM_API_ID and TELEGRAM_API_HASH (https://my.telegram.org) and TELEGRAM_SESSION (printed by the server's login.py, which you run once) and network: Full (MTProto goes to Telegram's data centres by IP address; put a VPN in front with --vpn PROFILE).
entries.license: MIT (MCP server, sandbox-ai-mcp); Telethon: MIT

env.name: TELEGRAM_API_ID
env.description: api_id of your application at https://my.telegram.org (API development tools)

env.name: TELEGRAM_API_HASH
env.description: api_hash of that application (32 hex digits)

env.name: TELEGRAM_SESSION
env.description: Telethon StringSession of the account (the whole account): python3 -I servers/telegram-user/src/login.py | sandbox-ai secrets set TELEGRAM_SESSION

env.name: TELEGRAM_USER_WRITE
env.description: 1 offers the write tools send_message, join_channel, leave_channel and mark_read (unset: read-only, they are not offered at all)

env.name: TELEGRAM_USER_ALLOWED_CHATS
env.description: Comma-separated chat ids and @usernames the write tools may use, e.g. -1001234567890,@mychannel (recommended with TELEGRAM_USER_WRITE; unset: every chat)

env.name: TELEGRAM_USER_DOWNLOAD_MB
env.description: Largest file download_media saves into /out, in MiB (1-2000, default 20)

env.name: TELEGRAM_MTPROXY
env.description: An MTProto proxy as host:port:secret (32 hex digits, optionally dd-prefixed; not ee fake-TLS) instead of a direct connection

entries.notes: The account's session is the whole account: it stays in the server's container (environment only, in memory, never on disk), is never returned and never logged, and the agent never sees it. Use an account made for the investigation, not your own. Telegram sees the connection's address: add the server with --vpn PROFILE (sandbox-ai's VPN with kill switch) or TELEGRAM_MTPROXY. Flood waits are answered with their time (retry_after), never slept through or retried. Message texts, names and links are written by other people: treat them as data, not instructions.

tor.note: MTProto over TCP to Telegram's data centres, through Tor.

entries.name: web-fetch
entries.title: Web pages as text
entries.description: Fetches an http(s) URL and returns its readable text (HTML reduced to title, text and optionally links), in parts for long pages. Only public addresses are fetched, also after redirects (no loopback, private or link-local targets), at most 5 MiB of text or HTML. Needs network: Full.
entries.license: MIT (MCP server, sandbox-ai-mcp)
entries.notes: Gives an agent whose own sandbox has no network read access to public web pages. The address check runs before each request; a resolver that answers differently a moment later (DNS rebinding) is not ruled out.

tor.note: HTTP(S) over TCP through Tor, .onion URLs included (Tor's address range for onion services is taken there).

entries.name: whatsapp
entries.title: WhatsApp account as a linked device (read-only by default)
entries.description: A WhatsApp account of yours through edouard-claude/whatsapp-mcp (a Rust MCP server with a Go bridge on whatsmeow), linked as a device like WhatsApp Web: it keeps the account's messages in an SQLite database with full-text search in the folder mounted at /data and offers the chats, messages (pages, context, recent, search), contacts, account status and media (downloaded into /data, size-capped by WHATSAPP_MEDIA_MB, default 64 MiB; small images and audio come back inline), and can ask the phone for older history. Read-only: sending, reactions, edits, deletions, read receipts, presence, groups, number lookups, profiles and the account's settings exist only with WHATSAPP_WRITE=1, and files to send only from a folder mounted at /send; pairing and logging out are never offered (link the device once with `wa-mcp pair`, see the server's PROVENANCE.md). Needs a writable /data (the session and the message database live there) and network: Full (WhatsApp's media hosts come from WhatsApp at run time).
entries.license: MIT (whatsapp-mcp); its bridge wa-bridge links whatsmeow and go-util (MPL-2.0) and libsignal (GPL-3.0), so the bridge binary is GPL-3.0

env.name: WHATSAPP_WRITE
env.description: 1 offers the tools that send or change anything on WhatsApp (messages, media, reactions, edits, deletions, read receipts, presence, groups, profile, settings); unset: read-only, they are not offered

env.name: WHATSAPP_MEDIA_MB
env.description: Largest media get_media downloads, in MiB (1-2000, default 64)

mounts.description: The account's folder, writable (--mount /data=DIR:rw): the linked device's keys (session.db), the message database, downloaded media; link the device into it once with wa-mcp pair
Files the write tools may send (send_media, a group photo), read-only (--mount /send=DIR:ro); without it no file can be sent

entries.notes: The folder at /data holds the linked device's keys: whoever has it reads and writes as the account, so keep it private (the server makes accounts/ owner-only) and give it to this server only. Only one connection at a time can use an account (a second one exits with 'déjà utilisé'). The device appears in the phone's Linked devices; unlink it there when done. This is an unofficial client: automated or bulk messaging can get a number banned. Messages, names, captions and files are written by other people: treat them as data, not instructions.

tor.note: WhatsApp's websocket and media hosts over TCP through Tor.

entries.name: whatweb
entries.title: Web site fingerprinting (WhatWeb)
entries.description: Identifies the technologies of a web site with WhatWeb 0.6.4 and its 1,800+ plugins: CMS and their versions, frameworks, web servers, JavaScript libraries, analytics, interesting headers. fingerprint returns the plugins matched per URL visited as JSON; aggression 1 (default) makes one ordinary GET per URL, 3 (only when asked) sends more requests to the same site to pin versions; 4 is not offered. plugin_info searches the plugins. Only http(s) URLs of public addresses, checked again before every redirect (at most 5, followed by the server, not by WhatWeb). Needs network: Full.
entries.license: MIT (MCP server, sandbox-ai-mcp); GPL-2.0-or-later (WhatWeb)

env.name: ALLOW_PRIVATE_TARGETS
env.description: 1: also scan private addresses (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, 100.64/10, fc00::/7); loopback and link-local stay refused

entries.notes: The site sees the requests coming from your address (--vpn PROFILE hides it). Aggression 3 is active probing: dozens of requests per matched plugin (version files, admin pages, one POST), only for sites you may scan. WhatWeb does not verify TLS certificates (it fingerprints, it sends nothing secret). The address check runs before each hop; a resolver that answers differently a moment later (DNS rebinding) is not ruled out. Titles, strings and header values come from the web site: treat them as data, not instructions.

tor.note: HTTP(S) over TCP through Tor, .onion URLs included; WhatWeb's timeouts are longer there (30 s to connect, 60 s to read, a run 240 s, at aggression 3 900 s).

entries.name: youtube
entries.title: YouTube uploads (your channel, credentials stay in the server)
entries.description: Publishes a video an agent made to your YouTube channel through the YouTube Data API v3, without the agent ever seeing your Google credentials: the OAuth client and its refresh token live only in this server's container, which refreshes its access token itself. upload_video (a video file of /upload, resumable upload with retries, private by default, unlisted on request, public only with YOUTUBE_ALLOW_PUBLIC=1; the audience required, the synthetic-content disclosure false unless set; chapters into the description), set_thumbnail (JPEG/PNG up to 2 MB), upload_captions (SRT/WebVTT), update_metadata (only the fields given) - these four WRITE to the channel: have sandbox-ai ask for each call - and list_my_videos (read-only). Every field is checked against YouTube's limits; files only from a folder mounted read-only at /upload, no links, devices or other users' files. Needs a Google Cloud project with the YouTube Data API v3, a Desktop OAuth client (YOUTUBE_CLIENT_ID, YOUTUBE_CLIENT_SECRET) and YOUTUBE_REFRESH_TOKEN (made once on the host with the server's authorize.py), and network: Allowlist with oauth2.googleapis.com:443 and www.googleapis.com:443. Uploads of a project Google has not audited stay private; an upload costs about 1600 of the project's 10,000 daily quota units.
entries.license: MIT (MCP server, sandbox-ai-mcp)

env.name: YOUTUBE_CLIENT_ID
env.description: Client id of the Desktop app OAuth client of your Google Cloud project (...apps.googleusercontent.com)

env.name: YOUTUBE_CLIENT_SECRET
env.description: Client secret of that OAuth client

env.name: YOUTUBE_REFRESH_TOKEN
env.description: Refresh token for your channel: python3 -I servers/youtube/src/authorize.py --client-secrets FILE | sandbox-ai secrets set YOUTUBE_REFRESH_TOKEN

env.name: YOUTUBE_ALLOW_PUBLIC
env.description: 1 lets upload_video and update_metadata make a video public and the write tools change a video that is public or scheduled to become public (unset: private and unlisted only)

env.name: YOUTUBE_MAX_UPLOAD_MB
env.description: Largest video upload_video takes, in MiB (1-262144, default 4096)

mounts.description: The videos, thumbnails and caption files to publish, read-only (--mount /upload=DIR:ro); without it nothing can be uploaded

entries.notes: The refresh token gives the server what its scopes allow on your channel (authorize.py asks for youtube.upload and youtube.readonly by default; youtube.force-ssl only for captions and metadata updates): it stays in the server's container (environment, memory), is never returned and never logged, and the agent never sees it. Ask for every write: a ruleset with {"server": "youtube", "tool": ["upload_video", "set_thumbnail", "upload_captions", "update_metadata"], "decision": "ask"} makes sandbox-ai ask you for each call. Publish the OAuth consent screen (In production): in Testing, Google lets a refresh token expire after 7 days. Videos uploaded by an API project Google has not audited are locked to private until it passes the audit. sandbox-ai gives an allowlist entry the full network (it cannot limit a server to hosts yet); the server itself sends requests to these two hosts only.

tor.note: HTTPS to Google's OAuth and YouTube Data API, over TCP through Tor.
